![](../assets/therapy/waterfall-jungle.jpg){.therapy-hero fig-alt=""}

## What the (Re-)Synchronising Therapy Method is

The (Re-)Synchronising Therapy Method, STM for short, is a form of psychological
and philosophical guidance for adults who are stuck with anxiety, low mood,
stress, tension, difficult experiences from the past, physical complaints without
a clear medical cause, or questions about identity and meaning.

The core idea is simple. Your inner life resembles music: all kinds of processes
in your body and mind play together. When they are well attuned, your experience
feels whole, coherent and alive. With complaints that attunement is disturbed;
you fall out of time, as it were. STM helps you restore that inner attunement, so
that you feel more whole, present and resilient again. Hence the word
"re-synchronising": coming back into sync.

STM is not a separate new technique. It is a way of working that brings proven
forms of therapy together (talking therapy, explanation and insight, movement and
body work, mindfulness, hypnotherapy, EMDR and short-term depth psychology) and
determines per person which of these, and in what order, help most.

The method is based on the [Resonance Theory of Consciousness](theory.qmd) (RTC),
the research on which the practitioner is writing his thesis.

STM is offered by an academically trained psychologist working independently and
autonomously. Read more under [About](about.qmd).

## The idea behind it, simply put

**Two ways of experiencing.** You can relate to your experience in two ways. The
first is direct experiencing: feeling what is here now, in your body and around
you, without immediately judging it. The second is thinking about it: naming,
judging, explaining, comparing, giving yourself a label. Both are needed. But
with complaints, thinking often takes over. You spend a lot of time "in your
head", you ruminate, you lose contact with direct feeling.

Old contemplative traditions have words for this. Avidya means "not-seeing":
losing contact with how your experience actually is. Dukkha means "suffering" or
"inner fragmentation": what follows from it. In this method we call the personal
form this takes in you the pathologos: the particular structure of your being
stuck. The psychological assessment at the start maps that structure.

**Rhythm and time.** Your experience has a rhythm. Under stress and anxiety that
rhythm speeds up; everything fragments, you feel rushed, you jump from one thing
to the next, you become exhausted. In low mood it slows down instead; everything
feels sluggish, flat and empty. STM helps bring your rhythm back to a more
comfortable pace, mainly through movement, breath and attention.

**Becoming whole again.** Recovery does not mean you will never feel anything
again, or that you will always be calm. It means you can move fluidly between
states again, that you have a stable sense of "now" that can also carry difficult
things, and that you are no longer stuck in the same groove.

## Who it is for, and when it is not

::: {layout-ncol=2}
::: {.card .p-4}
#### Suited to

Anxiety and panic, low mood and depressive complaints, chronic stress and
overstrain, the aftermath of difficult or overwhelming experiences, physical
complaints in which tension plays a part, rumination and worry, feelings of
estrangement or emptiness, and questions about who you are and what matters.
:::

::: {.card .p-4}
#### Not suited, or other care first

An acute crisis or strong thoughts of suicide, psychosis or untreated bipolar
disorder, a severe addiction that needs attention first, or a physical condition
that rules out exertion (in which case we adapt the movement component or refer
you). In those cases we look together at what you need now and refer you on where
appropriate. STM is not a crisis service.
:::
:::

## What a programme looks like

**1. Introduction and intake (two 60-minute sessions).** In the first
conversation we get acquainted and you map out your complaints, your background
and what you are asking for. In the second we discuss the questionnaire results,
I explain the model, and together we formulate your pathologos and your goals.
After that we make practical arrangements.

**2. Questionnaires.** At the start you complete three scientifically grounded
questionnaires: the NVM (on personality characteristics), the SCL-90 (on
complaints) and the UCL (on how you handle problems). They help us clarify the
nature and severity of your complaints and track your progress. We repeat the
complaints list a few times during the programme and at the end. A score is a
snapshot and a tool, not a stamp. Your data is treated confidentially in line
with privacy legislation.

**3. The treatment, in phases.**

- **Phase 1: calm and solid ground.** First we make sure you stand more firmly:
  explanation, breathing, grounding exercises, attention to sleep and lifestyle,
  and where needed a plan for difficult moments.
- **Phase 2: movement and presence.** We work with mindful movement and walking
  or running with attention, with breath and with mindfulness. This brings your
  rhythm back and strengthens contact with your body and the present moment.
- **Phase 3: loosening what is stuck.** Now we address the core: with talking
  therapy and short-term depth psychology we look at recurring patterns; with
  EMDR we process circumscribed difficult memories; with hypnotherapy and
  exercises we loosen stuck reactions.
- **Phase 4: anchoring.** We make sure what you have achieved lasts: freer
  movement, meaning and values, relapse prevention, and a calm tapering off with
  one or two follow-up appointments.

The phases do not run strictly one after another; we step back when needed and go
at your pace.

**4. A 60-minute session, step by step.**

| | |
|---|---|
| ± 5 min | briefly arriving and looking back on the past week |
| ± 5 min | setting the focus for today together |
| ± 5 min | a short exercise with breath, attention or body awareness to settle and make contact |
| ± 30 min | the actual work with one or two suitable techniques |
| ± 8 min | pausing at what it brought you and anchoring that |
| ± 5 min | taking home an exercise or assignment |
| ± 2 min | closing with a short check |

## The techniques we can use

We choose together what suits you. Possible are:

- **Talking therapy.** Exploratory conversations in which you come to understand
  yourself and your history better and start to recognise recurring patterns.
- **Explanation and insight (psycho-education).** Clear explanation about your
  complaints and about what helps, so that you gain more grip yourself.
- **Movement and body work ([MBMR](therapy.qmd)).** Walking or running with
  attention, rhythmic exercises and breath work, to restore your inner rhythm and
  strengthen contact with your body. This is a method of the practitioner's own
  research.
- **Mindfulness.** Training non-judgemental attention for the present moment;
  helps especially with rumination, stress and preventing relapse.
- **Hypnotherapy.** Working with a calm, inwardly directed state of attention to
  loosen stuck reactions and strengthen your inner resources. Always with your
  consent and under your direction.
- **EMDR.** A proven method for letting difficult memories lose their charge, in
  which you hold the memory while following eye movements or taps.
- **Short-term psychodynamic therapy.** A focused, time-limited form of depth
  psychology around a core theme.

## What can you expect as a result?

In the practitioner's practice, people who completed a full programme showed
broad relief of complaints: not only less of one complaint, but less anxiety, low
mood, physical tension, irritability and sleep problems at the same time. That
fits the idea behind the method: when the underlying coherence recovers, much
improves at once.

At the same time we are honest: there are no guarantees. How much you gain also
depends on your situation and on what you practise yourself between sessions. STM
does not replace your GP, a psychiatrist or medication; where needed we work
together with them. The integral framework of STM rests on a worked-out theory
and on practice-based research, but as a whole it has not yet been tested in
large comparative studies. The individual techniques we use have been.

## About the practitioner

Edward F. Hillenaar is an academically trained psychologist and philosopher. He
connects scientific psychology with philosophy and contemplative traditions and,
on the basis of his research — the Resonance Theory of Consciousness — developed
the MBMR and STM methods. He is working towards completing his thesis.

He works independently and autonomously, with his own integrative therapy method
grounded in his theory of consciousness. What that way of working involves and
whether it suits you, we discuss openly at the introductory meeting, so that you
can make an informed choice.

## Frequently asked questions

**Do I have to believe in something "spiritual"?** No. The method uses concepts
from philosophy and from contemplative traditions, but the treatment itself
consists of ordinary, recognisable psychological techniques.

**Do I have to be able to run for the movement part?** No. We start with walking
and build up at your pace. With physical limitations we adapt it.

**Is hypnotherapy safe? Will I lose control?** No. You remain conscious and in
charge throughout. Hypnosis is a form of concentrated attention; you do nothing
you do not want to do.

**Can I stop whenever I want?** Yes. You set the pace yourself and can always
discuss or end the programme.

**Does this also work alongside medication or treatment with a psychiatrist?**
Yes, that can go well together. With your consent we coordinate with your GP or
psychiatrist.

**How does the practitioner work?** As an academically trained psychologist,
independently and autonomously, with his own integrative therapy method grounded
in his research into consciousness. What that means precisely and whether it
suits you, we discuss openly at the introductory meeting.

## Important

::: {.callout-important}
STM is not a crisis service and is not available for emergencies. In acute
distress or with thoughts of suicide: call your GP or the out-of-hours GP
service, call 112, or call 113 Suicide Prevention (0800-0113, free, day and
night).
:::
